procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 23.02.2021, whereby the High Court rejected Criminal Petition No. 3788 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Petition No. 3788 of 2019 under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 28.05.2019 before the High Court to quash the FIR. On 07.08.2019, the High Court issued notice and granted an ad-interim direction staying further proceedings in the FIR as far as the appellant was concerned. However, the High Court ultimately dismissed the petition on 23.02.2021.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed Criminal Petition No. 3788 of 2019. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, finding that the complaint did not disclose any criminal offense and that the case was a purely civil dispute. The Supreme Court stated that allowing the police investigation to continue would be an abuse of the process of court and that the High Court erroneously refused to quash the FIR.

directions: The Impugned Judgment is set aside.
The FIR, as also any proceedings emanating therefrom, insofar as they relate to the appellant, are quashed and set aside.
Pending applications are consigned to records.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court should exercise its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to quash an FIR when the dispute is primarily of a civil nature and continuing the criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of court.

facts: The case involved a dispute over land ownership that was primarily civil in nature.
A criminal complaint (FIR) was filed after a significant delay (over 60 years) and only after the complainant had failed to get relief in civil court proceedings.
The appellant challenged the FIR in the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), but the High Court refused to quash it.
The appellant then appealed this refusal to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 482 of the CrPC grants High Courts inherent power to quash criminal proceedings.
This power should be exercised sparingly and with caution to prevent the abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice.

When deciding whether to quash an FIR, a court should consider two tests: (i) whether the allegations, taken at face value, prima facie constitute an offence, and (ii) whether the allegations are so improbable that a prudent person would not see sufficient grounds to proceed.
Using the judicial process for ulterior motives, vengeance, or to harass litigants is considered an abuse of process.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the complaint did not disclose any criminal offence and that the dispute was purely civil.
It observed that the criminal proceedings were initiated with ulterior motives after the complainant failed in the civil suits, effectively giving a "colour of criminality" to a civil dispute.
The Court found the complaint to be frivolous, vexatious, and oppressive.
It concluded that allowing the police investigation and criminal proceedings to continue would be a clear abuse of the process of law.
Therefore, the Court reasoned that this was a just and expedient case for the High Court to have exercised its "wholesome power" under Section 482 to quash the FIR.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred by not quashing the FIR. It held that when a dispute is fundamentally civil in nature and criminal proceedings are initiated with ulterior motives, allowing them to continue constitutes an abuse of the court's process. In such circumstances, the High Court should exercise its inherent power under Section 482 CrPC to quash the proceedings. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and quashed the FIR.

issue.issue_text: Whether the fact that an offense is covered under a 'special statute' inhibits the High Court or the Supreme Court from exercising their powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 or Article 142 of the Constitution.

facts: The case involves a legal question about the court's power to quash proceedings for an offense that falls under a 'special statute', specifically referencing the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (SC/ST Act).
law: The High Court possesses inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
The Supreme Court has extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice.
These powers are an exception, not the rule, and are to be exercised to prevent abuse of process or secure justice.
Special statutes, like the SC/ST Act, are stringent laws with serious penal consequences.
application: The Court relied on the precedent set by a 3-Judge Bench in the case of Ramawatar v State of Madhya Pradesh.
This precedent established that the court's powers under Section 482 CrPC and Article 142 are not automatically barred just because an offense is governed by a special statute.

The Court reasoned that it can still exercise these powers to quash proceedings, for example, when a settlement is reached, as long as the underlying objective of the special act is not contradicted or diminished.

The Court clarified that while the power to quash exists, law enforcement officers must be vigilant and not mechanically apply stringent statutes without due regard to the facts of the case, to avoid abuse of the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that the mere fact that an offense is covered under a 'special statute' does not inhibit the High Court or the Supreme Court from exercising their respective powers under Section 482 of the CrPC or Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court should refrain from exercising its power to quash an FIR on the ground that the matter involves disputed questions of fact that require police investigation.

facts: The State's counsel argued that the court should not intervene because the matter involved disputed questions of fact that required a police investigation.
The counsel also cited precedents holding that the power to quash an FIR should be used sparingly and that police should ordinarily be allowed to investigate.
law: The power of a court to quash an FIR under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to be exercised sparingly and with caution.
A court can quash an FIR if the uncontroverted allegations do not disclose the commission of any offense or are so improbable that a prudent person would not proceed with the complaint.
The general rule is that an FIR is meant to initiate the investigative process, and the police should ordinarily be allowed to investigate.
However, this general rule is not an absolute bar or "fetter" on the High Court or Supreme Court's power to quash an FIR in an appropriate case.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged the general principle that police should be allowed to investigate and that the court's power to quash is to be used cautiously.
However, the Court emphasized that this principle is not absolute and does not prevent the court from intervening in an "appropriate case."
The Court determined that the present case was one such appropriate case where it was necessary to invoke its "wholesome power" under Section 482 to prevent an abuse of the process of the court.

By finding that the High Court had erred in not quashing the FIR, the Supreme Court implicitly decided that the need for a police investigation into disputed facts was outweighed by the need to quash proceedings that were untenable in law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that it should refrain from exercising its power to quash the FIR. It held that while police should ordinarily be allowed to investigate matters involving disputed facts, this rule is not a fetter on the court's inherent power to intervene in an appropriate case to prevent an abuse of legal process. The Court found this to be such a case and proceeded to quash the FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court should exercise its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 to quash an FIR when the dispute is primarily of a civil nature and continuing the criminal proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of court.
appellant_arguments: The dispute is civil in nature, pointing to a civil suit from 2008 which was decreed against the complainant’s family members regarding the same property.
respondent_arguments: Under Section 482, the court only needs to determine if a cognizable offence is made out from the complaint, which it is in this case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the fact that an offense is covered under a 'special statute' inhibits the High Court or the Supreme Court from exercising their powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 or Article 142 of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The court's inherent power to quash proceedings is not barred by the invocation of a special statute. (This argument is implicit in the appellant's plea to quash the FIR which includes charges under the SC/ST Act).
respondent_arguments: The complainant belongs to the Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes category and is protected by the SC/ST Act, and the invocation of its provisions in the FIR was justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court should refrain from exercising its power to quash an FIR on the ground that the matter involves disputed questions of fact that require police investigation.
appellant_arguments: The court should consider facts showing the civil nature of the dispute, such as a prior civil suit decree, to determine if the criminal proceeding is an abuse of process.
respondent_arguments: The matter involves disputed questions of fact which the court should not go into.
The case should be left to be investigated by the police, who are already in the midst of the investigation.
The High Court should not act as an Investigating Officer.
Additional documents introducing new facts, which were not before the High Court, should not be considered.

statutes.principle: The Supreme Court's power under this article is not inhibited from being exercised even if the offense is covered under a 'special statute'.

The High Court's inherent power is not inhibited by a 'special statute' and can be exercised to (i) give effect to an order under the Code, (ii) prevent abuse of the process of court, and (iii) otherwise secure the ends of justice. The exercise of this power is an exception and not the rule.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mere fact that an offense is covered under a special statute does not inhibit the Supreme Court or the High Court from exercising their respective powers under Article 142 of the Constitution or Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: The exercise of power under Section 482 of the Code is an exception, not the rule, and it saves the inherent power the High Court already possessed.
Inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 may be exercised to give effect to an order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of court, or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.

All courts possess inherent powers, apart from express legal provisions, that are necessary for the proper discharge of their functions and duties, based on the principle that when the law gives something, it also gives that without which the thing cannot exist.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The criminal complaint and resulting FIR were quashed because the sequence of events demonstrated a malicious intent (mala fide) on the part of the complainant. Specifically, after a civil litigation concerning the same property had attained finality against the complainant's relatives, and after they failed to secure an interim order in a subsequent civil suit, the criminal complaint was registered. This indicates that the criminal proceedings were not a genuine grievance but an abuse of the court's process, initiated after failing to achieve the desired outcome through civil remedies.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.
The court is justified to quash any proceeding if it finds that the initiation or continuance of it amounts to an abuse of the process of court.

In appropriate cases, to prevent the judicial process from being an instrument of oppression or harassment in the hands of frustrated or vindictive litigants, the exercise of inherent power is not only desirable but necessary, so that the judicial forum may not be allowed to be utilized for any oblique motive.

When a complaint is sought to be quashed, it is permissible for the court to look into the materials to assess what the complainant has alleged and whether any offence is made out even if the allegations are accepted in toto.
policy_considerations: The authority of the court exists for the advancement of justice, and if any attempt is made to abuse that authority to produce injustice, the court has the power to prevent that abuse.
It would be an abuse of the process of the court to allow any action which would result in injustice and prevent the promotion of justice.
The power inhering in the High Court under Section 482 to prevent the abuse of process or to secure the ends of justice is a valuable safeguard for protecting liberty.
The court's inherent power is to be exercised 'ex debito justitiae' (as a matter of right, based on justice) to do real and substantial justice, for the administration of which alone courts exist.
